title: Can helpers beat cheats?
hook: Cheats win every single meeting with a helper. Can helping still take over?

knows: natural selection favours whatever scores best
in a one-off meeting, cheating beats helping
doesNotKnow: that in repeated meetings a reciprocal strategy (tit-for-tat) can beat always-cheat
that it only needs a small share to tip the population

objective: The learner can explain that with 10-round meetings tit-for-tat loses a little to each cheat but gains a lot with its own kind, so above about 1 in 17 (6%) of the population it scores more and takes over.

claims.text: In 10 rounds with payoffs 3/3 (both help), 0/5 (helper vs cheat) and 1/1 (both cheat), tit-for-tat scores 30 against itself and 9 against a cheat; a cheat scores 14 against tit-for-tat and 10 against a cheat.
claims.source: TFT vs TFT: 10 x 3 = 30. TFT vs cheat: round 1 gives 0 vs 5, rounds 2-10 give 1 each: 9 vs 14. Cheat vs cheat: 10 x 1 = 10.

claims.text: With random pairing and tit-for-tat share f, the two strategies score the same when 30f + 9(1 - f) = 14f + 10(1 - f), that is 21f + 9 = 4f + 10, f = 1/17, about 6%; above it tit-for-tat scores more.
On the stage, starting at 5% tit-for-tat falls to 1 of 100 by generation 60; starting at 7% it reaches 100 of 100 by generation 40.
claims.source: Deterministic imitation dynamics f' = f + f(1-f)(W_TFT - W_cheat)/15, clamped to 0..1, replicated in artifacts/scratch/w2life/pd.mjs. No random seed (grid positions only, untuned mulberry32(8)). The speed constant 15 is a choice; the tipping point does not depend on it.

claims.text: Reciprocal strategies such as tit-for-tat can invade and hold against always-defect when the same partners meet repeatedly.
claims.source: Axelrod R. & Hamilton W.D. (1981) The evolution of cooperation, Science 211:1390-1396.

claims.text: The model is a toy: two fixed strategies, chosen payoffs, exactly 10 rounds, random pairing in a very large population; it is not a claim about people.
claims.source: Model choice in Demo.tsx, stated on the stage and in the reveal.

recall.question: In repeated games, why can tit-for-tat take over from always-cheat once it is common enough?
options: It loses little to cheats and gains a lot when it meets its own kind
It beats a cheat in every meeting
recall.why: Against a cheat it loses only the first round; with another tit-for-tat it earns full cooperation. Once such meetings are common enough, its average beats the cheat's.
